---
title: "Handle malformed or untrusted input"
description: "Catch what zujson raises, tell the failures apart, and know the limits that bound the work."
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(zujson)
```

This guide is for code that parses a body it did not write: a response from
a service, a file a user uploaded. It shows how to catch a failure, how to
tell one kind from another, and which limits stop a hostile document from
exhausting the C stack or memory. It assumes you have read
`vignette("zujson")`.

## Catch every failure with one handler

Every condition the package raises inherits from `zujson_error`. Wrap the
call once, and nothing zujson raises escapes as a bare error:

```{r}
parse_or_null <- function(x) {
  tryCatch(json_parse(x), zujson_error = function(e) NULL)
}

parse_or_null('{"ok": true}')
parse_or_null("{bad")
```

## Tell the failures apart

In front of `zujson_error` sits a class that says what went wrong. Handle
the ones you can act on, and leave the rest to the general handler.

| Class | Raised when |
| --- | --- |
| `zujson_parse_error` | the input is not JSON, or is JSON that R cannot hold |
| `zujson_depth_error` | nesting goes past `zujson_info()$max_depth` levels |
| `zujson_limit_error` | `data_frame = TRUE` would build more than `zujson_info()$max_df_cells` cells |
| `zujson_io_error` | `json_parse_file()` cannot read the file |
| `zujson_write_error` | a value cannot be written, such as a date outside years 0000 to 9999 |
| `zujson_unsupported_type` | an R type has no JSON form, such as a complex or raw vector |
| `zujson_arg_error` | an argument is of the wrong type or length |

The class comes first in `class(e)`, and the message says where in the input
the problem is:

```{r}
e <- tryCatch(json_parse('{"a": }'), zujson_error = function(e) e)
class(e)
conditionMessage(e)
```

For NDJSON the message names the line, since a byte offset into ten thousand
records helps nobody:

```{r, error = TRUE}
json_parse_ndjson('{"id": 1}\n{"id": \n{"id": 3}\n')
```

## Do not rely on validating first

`json_validate()` answers "is this JSON?". That is nearly, but not exactly,
"will `json_parse()` succeed?". Two kinds of document are valid JSON and
still cannot become R values. The first is nesting deeper than the limit:

```{r}
deep <- paste0(strrep("[", 1500), strrep("]", 1500))

json_validate(deep)
class(tryCatch(json_parse(deep), zujson_error = function(e) e))[1]
```

The second is a string R cannot hold, such as one with an escaped NUL:

```{r}
nul <- '["a\\u0000b"]'

json_validate(nul)
class(tryCatch(json_parse(nul), zujson_error = function(e) e))[1]
```

So code that must not fail handles the condition from `json_parse()`. Use
`json_validate()` when the yes or no is all you need. `?json_validate` gives
the reasoning for both cases.

## The limits

`zujson_info()` reports the two limits in force, with the package and yyjson
versions:

```{r}
str(zujson_info())
```

**Depth.** Building the R value is recursive, so nesting is capped at
`max_depth` levels and a deeper document raises `zujson_depth_error` instead
of overflowing the C stack. The cap is compiled in. `json_validate()` does
not apply it, because the reader underneath is iterative and RFC 8259 leaves
the limit to the implementation.

**Data frame cells.** A data frame is rectangular, so records that share no
keys ask for one cell per record, per record: the size grows with the square
of the body. `max_df_cells` bounds the total for one document. Here a limit of 10
cells refuses three records that share no keys:

```{r, error = TRUE}
withr::with_options(list(zujson.max_df_cells = 10), {
  json_parse('[{"a":1,"b":1},{"c":1,"d":1},{"e":1,"f":1}]', data_frame = TRUE)
})
```

Set `options(zujson.max_df_cells = )` to raise or lower it for the session.

## Text must be UTF-8

Every string zujson returns is marked UTF-8, and that mark is true because
yyjson checked the bytes. Input that is not valid UTF-8 is refused, not
repaired:

```{r}
latin1 <- as.raw(c(0x22, 0xE9, 0x22)) # "é" in Latin-1, between quotes
json_validate(latin1)
```

Convert such input with `iconv()` before parsing. A leading UTF-8 byte order
mark is skipped and not refused, since real services send one.
